title: Oncall Playbook for Throttle and Backpressure Events
author: Anika Rao
body:
Summary:

This playbook defines the operational procedures for diagnosing, containing, and restoring services experiencing request throttling and internal backpressure. It covers first-responder actions, automated mitigations, escalation paths, customer-facing messaging templates, post-incident requirements, and recommended game-day exercises. The goal is to restore normal throughput while preserving data integrity and minimizing customer impact.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to service degradations where requests are being rejected, queued, or experiencing sustained elevated queue latency due to resource saturation or upstream/downstream throttles.
- Typical signals: elevated 5xx rates, rising queue length, worker OOMs, kernel-level I/O saturation, Redis/DB connection pooling exhaustion, or explicit 429 responses emitted by Redwood gateway or a dependency.
- Out-of-scope: routine rate limiting intentionally configured per-customer unless behavior is anomalous for that customer tier.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Acknowledge pager and set a temporary incident channel (Slack): #incident-<service>-throttle-<YYYYMMDD>.
2) Identify scope: Which regions, zones, clusters, and customer segments are affected? Use the dashboard filter: Service=/service-name, Region, Model, Route.
3) Confirm pager validity: Check alert triggers (thresholds breached and previous alert history).
4) Apply read-only guardrail: If possible, flip to circuit-breaker mode for the affected route to stop accepting new long-running requests while preserving short calls.
5) Capture timeline: note first observed metric, alert name, runbooks invoked, and the oncall(s) assigned.

Immediate containment options (choose applicable):
- Degrade non-critical features: disable batch-heavy endpoints, async background processes, and non-essential telemetry ingestion.
- Scale horizontally: increase worker replicas for stateless request processors if autoscaling is healthy and there's capacity. Command: kubectl -n prod scale deployment/<service> --replicas=<n> (verify capacity with capacity-dashboard first).
- Apply temporary global rate limit / token bucket: route-level config can be tightened for bursty clients. Example CLI: rdlctl routes update --route-id <id> --rate-limit 100rps.
- Drop low-priority queue consumers to free up connections to the database/cache.
- Fallback to a downstream-compatible model variant with lower memory/latency if model serving is the bottleneck.

Diagnostic queries and telemetry (examples to run immediately):
- Redis/Cache:
  * redis-cli -h <host> info stats; check instantaneous_ops_per_sec, blocked_clients, used_memory.
  * Monitor slowlog: redis-cli --latency-history 1000
- DB/Connection pool:
  * SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';
  * Check max_connections and peak usage in last 5m from pg-monitor.
- Kernel/IO:
  * iostat -x 1 5; look for %util > 80.
  * dstat or vmstat to check for swapping.
- Service-level metrics (PromQL examples):
  * Increase in 429s: sum(rate(http_responses_total{code="429",service="<svc>"}[1m])) by (route)
  * Queue latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_queue_duration_seconds_bucket{service="<svc>"}[5m])) by (le))
  * Worker OOMs: increase in kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}

Escalation matrix (time-based):
1) 0-10 minutes: Primary oncall (service owner).
2) 10-25 minutes: Secondary oncall / team SRE.
3) 25-45 minutes: Platform oncall + runtime performance lead.
4) 45+ minutes or customer-impacting outage: Pager duty escalation to ENG_MANAGER_ONCALL and notify Customer Success + Legal (if SLA breach likely).
Add names/roles in incident channel pinned message.

Decision tree: when to declare Severity 2 vs Severity 1
- Severity 2: Significant fraction of customers (>= 10%) experience degraded throughput but essential functionality remains. Latency SLO violation > 5 minutes and sustained 5xx/429 increases.
- Severity 1: Widespread outage where >50% requests failing for >2 minutes, or key customers are blocked and revenue-impacting SLAs are at risk.

Customer communications (templates)
- Short urgent status (use within first 30 minutes; aimed at CS and impacted customers):
Subject: [Redwood] Service disruption affecting request processing (short update)
Body: Hello — we are investigating an incident impacting request processing for some customers in <region>. We have activated our responders and are applying mitigations to restore throughput. We will provide another update within 30 minutes. Impact: increased request rejects (429) and elevated queue latency. No indication of data loss.
- Detailed status (post containment or 60-minute update):
Subject: [Redwood] Incident update — mitigation in place for request throttling
Body: Team — we identified elevated backpressure originating from <root cause summary>. We scaled workers and applied temporary rate limiting for non-critical routes. Impact: partial restoration for most customers; some batch routes remain degraded. Next update at <time>. If you are impacted, contact <support-contact> with your request IDs.
- Post-incident customer summary (after RCA):
Subject: [Redwood] Incident resolved — summary and follow-up actions
Body: The incident that impacted request processing between <start> and <end> has been resolved. Root cause: <one-line root cause>. Actions taken: scaled compute, adjusted pool sizes, and deployed patch to mitigate retry storm. Next steps: permanent config change planned for <date>. Compensation: customers affected for >X hours will receive credit per SLA terms.

Automated mitigations & quick remediations (runbook commands):
- Toggle circuit-breaker (API):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://control-plane/api/v1/routes/<route>/circuit-breaker -d '{"state":"open","reason":"incident-throttle"}'
- Increase replica count with safety:
  ./infra-tools scale-safe --service <svc> --target-replicas 12 --check-capacity true
- Temporarily disable heavy telemetry ingestion:
  kubectl -n obs patch deploy telemetry-ingestor --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/replicas","value":1}]'

Post-incident requirements (must be completed within 72 hours):
- Postmortem created in Confluence following the standard template (title: PM: <service> throttle <YYYY-MM-DD>) and linked to incident ticket.
- Action items assigned with owners and ETA.
- Telemetry retention extended for 7 days for all relevant metrics and traces.
- If SLO breached, prepare customer notice and propose credit as per finance policy.

Game-day and simulation guidance (recommended exercises):
- Quarterly tabletop: simulate a downstream DB connection pool exhaustion and walk through containment options. Duration: 90 minutes. Objectives: runbook familiarity, communications, and scaling checks.
- Live drill: in a staging environment, inject 20k concurrent synthetic requests to replicate queue growth and validate circuit-breaker behavior. Validate rollback procedures.
- Oncall rotation training: new oncall shadow for two weeks during which they run at least one simulated throttle incident under supervision.

Oncall ownership and runbook hygiene:
- Service owner: responsible for maintaining this playbook, verifying commands/monthly, and confirming reviewer list.
- SRE team: responsible for platform-level mitigations (scaling automation, cluster capacity dashboard).
- Documentation checklist (every 6 months): verify telemetry queries, update escalation contacts, and test CLI commands in staging.

SLOs and thresholds (summary table):
| Metric | Warning threshold | Alert threshold | Owner |
| HTTP 429 rate (svc-wide) | 0.5% of requests over 5m | 2% of requests over 1m | Service owner |
| Request queue 95th pctl | > 500ms for 10m | > 2s for 5m | Service owner |
| Worker OOM rate | 1 per hour | 3 per 10 minutes | Infra team |
| DB connection usage | > 70% capacity | > 90% capacity | DB team |

Postmortem template (minimum fields to include):
- Title
- Incident timeline (1-minute resolution)
- Scope & impact (customers, features, SLAs)
- Root cause analysis (evidence-backed)
- Immediate mitigations and why they worked/didn't
- Corrective actions (owners, ETA)
- Follow-up verification plan

Appendix A — common root cause patterns and recommended fixes:
- Retry storm: implement jittered exponential backoff and client-side capped concurrency. Review client SDK for aggressive retries.
- Connection pool exhaustion: increase pool size with connection multiplexing or move to connection pooling proxy.
- Memory leak in model-serving worker: roll back to previous model variant and run perf test; schedule a GC-profiler run.
- Disk IO saturation: offload logs/telemetry or increase IOPS/throughput on affected volumes.

Appendix B — links and references:
- Incident ticket template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-ticket-template
- Runbook automation tools: /confluence/eng-platform/automation-scripts
- Pager rotations: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations-directory
